issues.description: Experiment 1 started with 40 participants after training exclusions. The text states that 23 participants were included and 5 were excluded, but 23 + 5 = 28, not 40. Either 17 participants were excluded (40 - 23 = 17), or the number of included participants is incorrect. This discrepancy makes it impossible to evaluate the actual exclusion rate and its impact on generalizability.
issues.quote: Exclusion of participants with too few high confidence critical trials in one or more cells of the design (10 trials or less) were excluded from the analysis resulted in an inclusion of 23 participants (5 participants were excluded) when the results were averaged across the set size conditions.

issues.description: In Experiment 1, the Methods section describes a 2-point confidence scale (1 = guess, 2 = certain), but the Figure 1 caption describes a 4-point confidence scale (1 = guess, 4 = certainty). This is a direct contradiction that affects interpretation of what constitutes 'high confidence' responses—the entire dependent variable of interest.
issues.quote: They were instructed to select "none of these" if the target letter was not a response option. After selecting the target letter, participants indicated their confidence by clicking on one of two boxes (from 1-2, 1 = guess, 2 = certain).

issues.description: For Experiment 2's follow-up ANOVA on non-illusory errors (Table 4), the text states 'BFincl = 190 for Memory Delay' and that 'only Memory Delay was a relevant factor.' However, Table 4 shows BFincl = 0.064 for Memory Delay (evidence against inclusion) and BFincl = 39,110.895 for Target Type (overwhelming evidence for inclusion). The text and table are directly contradictory. Either the table rows are mislabeled or the text is reporting wrong values. This affects the interpretation of whether non-illusory errors increase with memory delay.
issues.quote: For other, non-illusory errors only Memory Delay was a relevant factor (BFm = 42, see Appendix 1 for a full model comparison and Table 4 for an overview of BFincl for each model component). Non-illusory error rates increased from the short to the long delay (BFincl = 190 for Memory Delay)

issues.description: Experiment 4's results section refers to 'Figure 5' for the error rates, but Figure 5 is the figure for Experiment 3. Based on the sequential numbering, Experiment 4's figure should be Figure 6, which is indeed captioned for Experiment 4 later in the text.
issues.quote: Figure 5 shows the error rates for high confidence trials. A Bayesian repeated measures ANOVA model comparison showed that the model with main effects for Error Type, Target Type, Memory Delay...

issues.subcategory: Inconsistent delay description in General Discussion
issues.description: The General Discussion states 'Illusory memories make up almost 20% of reports when memory is probed at 500 ms (Experiment 1 and 2).' However, Experiment 1's Short condition probed memory at 750 ms after memory display offset, not 500 ms. Only Experiments 2 and 4 had a 500 ms probe delay.
issues.quote: Illusory memories make up almost 20% of reports when memory is probed at 500 ms (Experiment 1 and 2)

issues.description: For Experiments 2-4, which use a 4-point confidence scale, the manuscript never specifies which confidence ratings qualify as 'high confidence.' The entire analysis depends on separating high- from low-confidence trials, yet the reader cannot determine whether high confidence means ratings of 4 only, ratings of 3-4, or some other threshold. This is critical for replicability and interpretation.
issues.quote: then indicated her confidence (on a scale from 1 - 4)

issues.description: Exclusion rates based on insufficient high-confidence trials are very high: potentially up to 42.5% in Experiment 1 (17/40), 31.7% in Experiment 2 (92/290). These exclusion rates raise serious concerns about selection bias, as the analyzed sample consists only of participants who were frequently highly confident—a subgroup that may not be representative. No analysis examines whether excluded participants differ from included ones on task-relevant dimensions beyond confidence frequency.
issues.quote: Exclusion of participants with too few high confidence trials in one or more cells of the design (10 trials or less) resulted in an inclusion of 198 participants (92 participants were excluded)

issues.subcategory: Temporal increase does not rule out encoding-based explanation
issues.description: The authors argue that the increase in illusory errors over time rules out a perceptual encoding explanation. However, this logic is incomplete. If perceptual encoding of pseudo-letters produces a noisier or more ambiguous representation than encoding of real letters, such representations could degrade more rapidly over time. The increase in errors over delay intervals could reflect differential decay of weakly encoded traces rather than an active memory illusion process. The temporal increase is therefore consistent with both memory-based and encoding-quality-based accounts.
issues.quote: If the illusions are simply the result of misperceptions, their frequency of occurrence should remain the same over the time-course of STM – since in all cases initial perceptual inference has been completed.

issues.subcategory: High confidence conflated with vivid memory experience
issues.description: The authors use high confidence as a proxy for having an actual (albeit false) memory trace, as opposed to guessing. However, high confidence can also reflect strong prior expectations being applied during retrieval with high certainty, without necessarily reflecting a vivid memory experience. A participant who has no memory trace but is very confident that letters appear in their normal orientation would also give a high-confidence incorrect response. The confidence measure cannot distinguish between these possibilities.
issues.quote: isolating high confidence responses is necessary to identify those responses that reflect a participant having an actual, albeit false, memory of perceiving something that was not there.

issues.description: The authors dismiss response bias in Experiment 1's discussion without adequate evidence, stating only that 'the pattern of responses across conditions is consistent with memory-driven processes rather than response bias.' However, a response bias toward selecting real letters could also increase over time as memory becomes less certain and participants increasingly fall back on default preferences. The interaction with delay does not uniquely support a memory illusion over a response bias that becomes more influential as memory weakens.
issues.quote: However, this is unlikely because the pattern of responses across conditions is consistent with memory-driven processes rather than response bias.

issues.subcategory: Mischaracterization of Fuzzy Trace Theory prediction
issues.description: The authors state that FTT predicts high similarity should facilitate false memories, and claim this is 'not consistent with the current data' because false memories are abundant despite high similarity. But abundant false memories for highly similar items is exactly what FTT would predict. The authors appear to confuse FTT's prediction about similarity with the directional asymmetry they observe. The asymmetry is what FTT cannot easily explain (since visual similarity is symmetric), but the way the argument is phrased incorrectly suggests that FTT's prediction is disconfirmed by the mere presence of false memories.
issues.quote: However, FTT predicts that high similarity between a target and its mirrored counterpart should facilitate false memories. This is not consistent with the current data: The mirrored counterpart (the real letter) and the target (the pseudo-letter) are extremely similar, yet false memories are abundant.

issues.description: No effect sizes (e.g., η², Cohen's d, or credible intervals) are reported for any of the analyses across all four experiments. Only Bayes Factors are reported. Effect sizes are necessary to evaluate the practical significance of the findings and to allow for future meta-analyses or power calculations.

Experiments 3 and 4 used sequential testing with Bayesian stopping rules, but with different BF thresholds (BF > 6 for Experiment 3; BF > 10 for Experiment 4). No justification is provided for why different thresholds were used. Additionally, the frequency of checking ('every other day of testing') introduces variability in effective stopping points depending on enrollment rates.
issues.quote: Every other day of testing, the sequential analysis was run, and once the outcome crossed a BF of 6, testing would stop.

issues.description: There is no mention of pre-registration for any of the four experiments. Experiments 1 and 2 do not have stopping rules or pre-specified analysis plans mentioned. Given the multiple possible analysis choices (exclusion criteria, confidence thresholds, whether to collapse across conditions), the absence of pre-registration is a concern for analytic flexibility.

Experiment 4 was conducted online with participants using their own laptops, introducing uncontrolled variability in display size, resolution, viewing distance, and ambient lighting. For a visual memory task involving letter discrimination, these factors could affect stimulus discriminability and thus encoding quality. This is not acknowledged as a limitation.
issues.quote: the data was collected in an online experiment, using Neurotask scripting. Participants that signed up to take part in the experiment were invited to join a Zoom meeting at a preset time.

issues.subcategory: Unequal trial proportions in Experiment 1 response displays
issues.description: In Experiment 1, the probability of the target appearing in the response display differed between real letters (83%) and pseudo-letters (50%), and the probability of the mirrored counterpart appearing also differed. This creates an asymmetric response environment that could contribute to differential error patterns. While the authors acknowledge this and address it in Experiment 2, the initial interpretation of Experiment 1's asymmetric illusion rates is potentially confounded.
issues.quote: If the target was a pseudo-letter, then it appeared as a response option randomly on half of those trials while on the other half of pseudo-letter trials only the real counterpart was one of the response options. If the target was a real letter, then it appeared as a response option on a randomly selected 83% of the trials

issues.description: In Experiment 1, the three-way interaction between Target Type, Error Type, and Memory Delay has only anecdotal evidence (BFincl = 2.45), yet the authors proceed to describe and interpret the specific pattern of this interaction in detail, reporting percentage differences for each condition. Interpreting an effect that is not well-supported by the model comparison undermines the Bayesian analytical framework the authors chose.
issues.quote: Finally, there is only anecdotal evidence for a three-way interaction between Target Type, Error Type and Memory Delay (BFincl = 2.45): For pseudo-letter targets, illusory errors increase 12% as memory deteriorates

issues.description: The manuscript states that symmetric letters were excluded but does not list the full set of letters that were used in the experiments. Knowing the specific letter set is important because some asymmetric letters have more visually distinct mirror images than others, which could affect error rates differentially. This omission hinders replicability.
issues.quote: Therefore only letters that changed when mirrored were included in the experiment (i.e. the symmetrical letters A,H,I,M,O,T,U,V,W,X,Y were excluded from the memory and response displays).

issues.description: Different letters have different degrees of visual asymmetry when mirrored (e.g., 'b' vs 'd' are highly confusable, while other mirrored letters may be more distinctive). No analysis is reported examining whether the illusion rates vary across specific letters. Item-level variability could drive or inflate the observed effects if certain highly confusable letter pairs dominate the illusion rate.

All four experiments use only mirrored letters as stimuli. The authors make broad claims about STM being susceptible to illusions driven by 'world knowledge,' but the findings are limited to a single, highly specific stimulus domain (letter orientation). Generalization to other forms of world knowledge or other visual features is speculative and insufficiently qualified.
issues.quote: Together, these experiments show that expectations can reshape perceptual representations over short time scales, leading to what we refer to as short-term memory (STM) illusions.

issues.description: Experiments 2-4 rely on first-year psychology students participating for course credit. This sample may have particularly strong letter representations due to recent academic engagement. The authors do not discuss whether the observed effects might be modulated by literacy level, age, or familiarity with the Latin alphabet.
issues.quote: The participants participated for student credits as part of a course within the first-year Psychology curriculum.

issues.description: In Experiment 1, participants were trained on a rectangle orientation change detection task, which differs substantially from the main letter memory task. The training serves as a screening tool, but the relevance of performance on a rectangle task for predicting letter memory ability is unclear, and the exclusion based on this unrelated task may not effectively screen for the intended competency.
issues.quote: Prior to the main experiment, participants were trained on a cued change detection task. In this training task, participants were instructed to indicate whether the rectangle at a cued location in a memory display had the same orientation as the rectangle at that same location in a test display.

issues.subcategory: Confound between delay and interference timing
issues.description: In Experiment 1, the three conditions confound delay duration with interference timing. In the Short condition, the irrelevant display appears 5 seconds after memory onset; in the Long condition, it also appears at 5 seconds but after the cue; in the Short-with-interference condition, it appears with the cue at 0.75 seconds. The timing of the irrelevant display relative to both the memory display and the cue varies across conditions, making it difficult to attribute differences solely to memory delay or interference.
issues.quote: If the memory probe appeared in isolation (the Short and Long conditions), the irrelevant second display appeared 5 seconds after memory display offset, which meant that the interval between the probe and the irrelevant second display was either presented for 1.5s (Long delay) or 3.75s (short delay).

issues.subcategory: Missing degrees of freedom and sample descriptives per analysis
issues.description: The Bayesian ANOVAs are reported without degrees of freedom, and the exact number of participants contributing to each analysis cell is not always clear (especially given the exclusion procedures and listwise deletion). For Experiment 3, an additional participant was excluded via listwise deletion but this is only mentioned in passing.
issues.quote: Because of listwise deletion of missing values (resulting from 0 high confidence responses in one or more of the cells of the design), one participant was excluded from the main ANOVA.

issues.description: By focusing exclusively on high-confidence trials and excluding participants with too few such trials, the authors discard a substantial portion of the data. No analysis is reported on low-confidence trials to verify that the pattern differs (e.g., that illusions are less prevalent at low confidence). Such an analysis would strengthen the claim that high confidence specifically indexes illusory memories rather than guessing.
issues.quote: Exclusion of participants with too few high confidence critical trials in one or more cells of the design (10 trials or less) were excluded from the analysis

issues.description: The authors do not conduct signal detection analyses (e.g., computing d' and criterion/beta) to formally separate sensitivity from response bias. Given that one of the central claims is that the effects are not due to response bias, a signal detection framework would provide much stronger evidence than the informal argument currently provided.
issues.quote: Yet another reason why illusory reports arise could be a response bias: Participant might just be more inclined to select real letters instead of pseudo-letters, since real letters are a well-known category. However, this is unlikely because the pattern of responses across conditions is consistent with memory-driven processes rather than response bias.

issues.subcategory: Accuracy rates for correct responses not fully reported
issues.description: The manuscript focuses on error rates but does not systematically report overall accuracy rates or correct response rates across conditions for all experiments. Without knowing how overall performance varies across conditions and target types, it is difficult to contextualize the error rates and determine whether the illusion pattern reflects changes in errors or changes in overall difficulty.

issues.subcategory: Overly strong claim that IM is not tested
issues.description: The authors claim their experiments do not test iconic memory because the shortest probe delay is 500-750ms. However, some researchers define iconic memory as lasting up to 1 second, and the 500ms condition in Experiments 2 and 4 could plausibly tap into iconic or post-iconic stages. The claim that IM is untested is stated too definitively given the temporal overlap.
issues.quote: Our experiments currently do not test whether illusory memories arise in IM, which is sometimes thought not to be susceptible to illusions based on contextual information or internally generated biases.

issues.description: In Experiment 1, results are described as 'averaged across the set size conditions' without pre-specifying this collapsing. Set size (6 vs 8 items) could modulate the illusion rate, and collapsing obscures potential interactions. Similarly, in Experiment 2, data are collapsed across cue color after finding no effect, but this was not the pre-specified primary analysis plan.
issues.quote: resulted in an inclusion of 23 participants (5 participants were excluded) when the results were averaged across the set size conditions
